prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture that he has declined, in an anticoagulated patient, when amyloid PET answers the same question.
Do not stop anticoagulation for two strictly deep microbleeds in a patient with atrial fibrillation and no falls [ESC_AF_2024].
Do not keep edoxaban at 60 mg once daily without checking the creatinine clearance.
Do not attribute the dementia to atrial fibrillation when there is no infarct on MRI.
Do not prescribe anticholinergic bladder agents alongside a cholinesterase inhibitor.
Do not attribute the gait disturbance to the dementia when neurogenic claudication and absent ankle jerks explain it.
required_recommendations: Name the diagnosis as mixed dementia: Alzheimer disease (storage-type amnesia, MTA grade 3, positive amyloid PET) with a small-vessel vascular contribution (Fazekas 2, three lacunes, two deep microbleeds) [VASCOG_2014].

Answer the family's question directly: after six years of anticoagulated atrial fibrillation the MRI shows no cortical or territorial infarct, so the arrhythmia is not causing the dementia; the vascular part is small-vessel disease.

Reduce edoxaban to 30 mg once daily and continue anticoagulation: Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance is about 46 mL/min (age 81, 71 kg, creatinine 1.28 mg/dL), within the 15-50 mL/min band; CHA2DS2-VA is 3, and two deep microbleeds without falls do not outweigh the benefit [ESC_AF_2024].

Offer a cholinesterase inhibitor for the Alzheimer component (e.g. donepezil 5 mg at night, increased to 10 mg after 4-6 weeks if tolerated), checking heart rate and ECG before and after starting because diltiazem slows AV conduction and raises donepezil exposure [NICE_NG97].
Lower blood pressure gradually to below 130/80 mmHg (152/78 on ramipril and diltiazem), checking orthostatic blood pressure at each change, which tamsulosin makes more likely to fall [ESO_2021_SVD].
Attribute the absent ankle jerks, distal sensory loss and claudication-limited gait to the lumbar stenosis, not to the dementia.
Support his daughter as carer: supervised medication, finances and advance care planning, with review of cognition and function in 6-12 months [NICE_NG97].

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role here: the course is gradual over three years, with no fluctuation, episodes or rapid progression.
No spontaneous parkinsonism, fluctuating alertness, hallucinations or dream enactment: a dopamine transporter scan answers no question in this patient.
No core feature of Lewy body disease; cardiac sympathetic imaging answers no question in this patient.
A gradual three-year amnestic decline is not the subacute multidomain syndrome that indicates paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitis antibodies.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
No cortical or territorial infarct and the atrial fibrillation is already anticoagulated: an echocardiogram would not change the diagnosis or the antithrombotic plan.
Atrial fibrillation is already documented and anticoagulated; prolonged rhythm monitoring changes neither the diagnosis nor the treatment.
Mr Riva has declined lumbar puncture and takes edoxaban, which would need interrupting; amyloid PET answers the same question.

accepted: Mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia: amyloid-PET-confirmed Alzheimer pathology with moderate hypertensive small-vessel disease

differential.key_features: Storage-type amnesia, MTA grade 3 and a positive amyloid PET establish Alzheimer pathology, but Fazekas 2 white matter disease with three lacunes is a second contributor with treatable risk factors; Alzheimer disease alone would leave it untreated
Six years of anticoagulated atrial fibrillation with no cortical or territorial infarct on MRI: the family's hypothesis is reasonable and the imaging refutes it
A storage-type amnesia unresponsive to cueing with Scheltens 3 atrophy is not produced by a Fazekas 2 burden

Evans index 0.30 with disproportionate temporal horn enlargement is the atrophy pattern, the gait is limited by neurogenic claudication rather than magnetic, and there is no disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space

differential.key_features: The lumbar stenosis and previous laminectomy explain the claudication, absent ankle jerks and distal sensory loss, but have no bearing on cognition

key_clinical_evidence: Amyloid PET and CSF answer the same question, and the choice between them is a patient-level decision: he has declined lumbar puncture, takes edoxaban and has had spinal surgery
Absence of cortical infarction after six years of anticoagulated atrial fibrillation is evidence that the arrhythmia is not the mechanism, and it answers the family's question with data
Microbleed distribution decides the anticoagulation question: strictly deep means hypertensive arteriopathy and does not overturn the indication, whereas lobar microbleeds with siderosis would
A coexisting spinal problem can account for gait and reflex findings without contributing anything to the cognitive diagnosis, and conflating them wastes investigation
Naming mixed disease produces two treatment plans; naming one leaves the other untreated
DOAC dosing follows Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance: at 81 years, 71 kg and creatinine 1.28 mg/dL the clearance is about 46 mL/min, which sets edoxaban at 30 mg

alternatives: Rivastigmine (not metabolised by CYP450) avoids the pharmacokinetic component but shares the bradycardia warning.
interactions: Donepezil with diltiazem: additive slowing of heart rate and AV conduction (cholinesterase inhibition plus a non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker); risk of bradycardia, AV block and syncope. Diltiazem is a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor and may modestly raise donepezil exposure.
Donepezil with tamsulosin: no pharmacokinetic interaction; both can contribute to dizziness and falls.
Donepezil with edoxaban, ramipril or atorvastatin: no clinically relevant interaction.
donepezil.summary: Moderate interaction between donepezil and diltiazem (bradycardia and AV block, with a modest rise in donepezil exposure); usable with heart-rate and ECG monitoring.
warnings: Record resting heart rate and a 12-lead ECG before the first dose and after each dose increase; review the combination if the resting rate falls below about 55/min or syncope, presyncope or falls occur.
Antimuscarinic bladder agents oppose the effect of a cholinesterase inhibitor and add anticholinergic burden.

interactions: Edoxaban with diltiazem: diltiazem is a moderate CYP3A4 and weak P-glycoprotein inhibitor; no edoxaban dose change is required (the label reduces the dose only with strong P-gp inhibitors such as ciclosporin, dronedarone, erythromycin or ketoconazole).
Edoxaban with ramipril, atorvastatin or tamsulosin: no clinically relevant interaction.
Edoxaban with aspirin, NSAIDs or SSRIs: increased bleeding risk.
edoxaban.summary: No dose-relevant interaction with diltiazem. Edoxaban dose depends on creatinine clearance and body weight.
warnings: Dose by Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance, not eGFR: 60 mg once daily when CrCl is above 50 mL/min; 30 mg once daily when CrCl is 15-50 mL/min, body weight is 60 kg or less, or a strong P-gp inhibitor is co-prescribed.
Recheck renal function at least yearly, and more often when CrCl is below 60 mL/min.

alternatives: Donepezil and rivastigmine share the class bradycardia warning.
interactions: Galantamine with diltiazem: additive bradycardia and AV block; diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4 and may raise galantamine exposure.
Galantamine with edoxaban, ramipril, atorvastatin or tamsulosin: no clinically relevant interaction.
Galantamine clearance falls with renal impairment; titrate slowly with reduced creatinine clearance.
galantamine.summary: Moderate interaction between galantamine and diltiazem (bradycardia, raised galantamine exposure); usable with monitoring.
warnings: Record resting heart rate and a 12-lead ECG before starting and after each dose step.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Alberto Riva is an 81-year-old retired notary clerk who attends with his daughter. She describes three years of gradual decline, memory first: he forgets conversations within the hour, has lost the thread of the family finances he used to keep, and now needs prompting to take medication. There have been no abrupt steps she can date and no episodes of weakness or speech loss. In the last year he has begun to lose words. He has had atrial fibrillation for six years and has been reliably anticoagulated on edoxaban. His daughter's specific question is whether the atrial fibrillation is 'causing small strokes'. He also has lumbar stenosis with neurogenic claudication and long-standing numb feet, and a laminectomy eight years ago. He declines a lumbar puncture when it is offered, both because of the previous spinal surgery and because he is anticoagulated. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness and no dream enactment. His blood pressure runs at 150 systolic.

neurological_exam.additional: Pulse irregularly irregular at 78. No frontal release signs. No parkinsonian features.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Visual fields full. Face symmetric. Speech fluent with word-finding pauses.
neurological_exam.gait: Stooped and cautious with reduced step length, limited by neurogenic claudication after 200 metres; arm swing preserved. Uses a stick.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and cooperative; oriented to person and place, year correct, month and date incorrect. Slow to find words; conversation coherent. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk with mild distal wasting in the legs. Tone normal. Strength 5/5 proximally, 4+/5 ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally, attributed to the lumbar stenosis.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ knees, absent ankle jerks, plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reduced vibration at the ankles with a patchy L5-S1 distribution of sensory loss, long-standing.
